title: White House blocks Politico from Air Force One amid press access lawsuit
content: The White House is refusing to allow Politico on Air Force One on Monday, which means the news organization cannot fulfill its press corps pool responsibilities. A Politico spokesperson confirmed that the publication was excluded from the out-of-town travel pool, a small group of reporters who travel with the president on trips. President Donald Trump announced on September 18 that he was “banning” Politico, CNN and MS NOW from the White House, a move that legal experts called unconstitutional. The news outlets filed a lawsuit on September 21 alleging the ban violates the First and Fifth Amendments. Judge Timothy J. Kelly sided with the plaintiffs and issued a temporary restraining order requiring the Trump administration to reinstate the journalists’ press badges. Since then, however, the White House has repeatedly barred CNN from traveling on Air Force One on days when it has been CNN’s turn to be the TV pool representative. Now, on the day it was Politico’s turn to be the print pool representative, Politico has been barred as well. The Trump administration appears to be justifying these new restrictions by saying that access to the White House complex is different than access to tight spaces like Air Force One. The Associated Press has an ongoing lawsuit over this distinction, since Trump tried to ban the wire service from certain spaces last year. Monday’s action against Politico will likely be incorporated into the next legal filing by CNN, MS NOW and Politico. Judge Kelly is scheduled to hold a hearing on Thursday over the news outlets’ request for a preliminary injunction, which would protect press access to the White House for a longer period of time ahead of a potential trial. “The law is absolutely clear. The harm to our clients, the First Amendment, and the public as a whole is profound,” the attorney for the three news outlets, Ted Boutrous, said in a statement. “It is critical that the White House is enjoined to keep this unconstitutional ban on the free press out of commission.” Last week, when reporters from TIME asked if Trump was ignoring the court order, Trump said no, and then communications director Steven Cheung piped in: “The judge basically ordered them to renew their access back to the White House, but that’s different than allowing the pool into the events in the Oval Office or on Air Force One.” Cheung did not respond to a request for comment on Monday about the action against Politico. Trump is slated to travel to Nebraska for a campaign stop on Monday afternoon. With Politico barred from the trip, the White House offered the publication’s seat to other news organizations that routinely take turns in the out-of-town travel pool, and several publications declined, sources with knowledge of the matter told CNN. Unusually, the White House’s Sunday night guidance email to the press corps did not list any news outlets traveling with the president at all — perhaps a sign that Politico’s seat was proving hard to fill.

title: Mark Thompson to remain CNN chairman as Ellisons take control of Warner Bros. Discovery
content: Mark Thompson, who has led CNN for the past three years, will remain at the helm as the Ellison family acquires the news network’s parent company, Warner Bros. Discovery. With the merger of Paramount and Warner set to take effect Tuesday, the combined company, named Skydance , announced its leadership team on Monday morning. Thompson will stay in place as chairman and editor-in-chief of CNN, reporting to Skydance CEO David Ellison and co-CEO Ynon Kreiz. The announcement resolved months of uncertainty relating to the politically charged media mega-merger. It also signaled that there won’t be any immediate combination of CNN with Paramount’s CBS News unit. In a memo to CNN staffers on Monday, Thompson wrote, “First, I’m convinced that from David Ellison on down, Paramount Skydance leadership really does believe in news alongside entertainment as a top strategic opportunity for our new company. They’ve seen our digital strategy and are as excited about it as we are.” “And second, having now spoken to them at length on the topic, I have real confidence that they both understand and will fully support the principle and practice of the kind of independent news that CNN has always stood for,” Thompson wrote. “That’s why I will be leading CNN into this new chapter as it becomes one of Skydance’s suite of major media assets and global brands, and leading it as an independent editor-in-chief with the same responsibilities and prerogatives that I have now.” Thompson, who ran the BBC and The New York Times Co. before joining CNN in 2023, held several meetings with Paramount executives last week, sources familiar with the matter said on condition of anonymity. The Wall Street Journal was the first to report that David Ellison had asked Thompson to stay on, auguring stability for CNN at a volatile time for the news media. When Paramount won the bidding war for Warner last February, CNN employees expressed serious concerns about whether the Ellisons would uphold editorial independence at one of the biggest news organizations in the world. Paramount patriarch Larry Ellison, one of the richest men in the world, has been a close ally of President Donald Trump, who said last December that “it’s imperative that CNN be sold.” Trump signaled that he viewed the change in ownership as a way for him to exert control over news coverage, and so have his allies. “The sooner David Ellison takes over that network, the better,” Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said last March. Trump, Hegseth and other officials attended an off-the-record dinner with David Ellison and other Paramount leaders in April. Officials in Trump’s Justice Department green-lit the merger in June despite misgivings from career staffers, according to the Journal. David Ellison’s changes at CBS News also caused consternation. Shortly after acquiring Paramount in August 2025, he acquired The Free Press website and installed co-founder Bari Weiss as CBS News editor-in-chief. Weiss-led shakeups in the network news division prompted months of bad press, allegations of managerial ineptitude, and rumblings that Ellison had miscast her in the role. Several ousted correspondents accused Weiss of unduly interfering with their work, though Weiss denied that. While key CBS newscasts have continued to struggle in the ratings, Weiss and her deputies have notched numerous reporting wins and launched new ventures, including podcasts and live events. And despite Paramount’s attempts to put on a Trump-friendly face, CBS News has kept breaking hard-hitting stories, including about the Trump administration. During the Warner merger tug-of-war, David Ellison praised CNN and said that “editorial independence will absolutely be maintained.” Still, many merger opponents warned that the Ellison family couldn’t be trusted with a news asset like CNN. Some of the Democratic state attorneys general who filed an antitrust suit in July to block the deal were openly critical of Weiss and her actions at CBS. Monday’s announcement said Weiss will remain in charge at CBS News, which will continue to operate separately from CNN for the time being. Some cross-pollination between CNN and CBS News, and maybe even a full-blown merger of the news divisions, is still expected eventually, however. “The specifics of how CNN will plug into and operate in the new company have yet to be finalized — hardly surprising given that serious discussions could only begin after Paramount’s anti-trust settlement a few days ago,” Thompson wrote in his memo. Those discussions will surely involve how to bring CNN and CBS News closer together and — even more urgently — how to keep growing digital businesses to offset cable and broadcast declines. For now, there are many unknowns, including how the court-mandated “editorial independence board” will fit into all this. When the state attorneys general agreed to settle their antitrust lawsuit on September 21, the settlement called for creating a five-member board overseeing CBS News and CNN. The board is meant to uphold editorial standards and resolve disputes, according to the settlement terms. Skydance has not yet appointed the board members, and it has six months to do so. Once the merger takes effect on Tuesday, Skydance will face severe pressure to cut costs, since the combined company has been saddled with an enormous amount of debt. At the same time, Skydance will rely on the cash flow from profitable channels like CNN to support its restructuring, giving it good reason to avoid disrupting the network while growing its digital businesses. Thompson wrote in his memo, “I know many of you have had trepidations about this moment. That’s understandable — indeed, as I’ve hinted before, I’ve had the odd moment or two myself! But I want to say that on the eve of the acquisition of CNN by Paramount Skydance, I find myself in a very positive frame of mind. I really do believe we’ll be working alongside a team who don’t just have real vision and real energy, but real values as well.” Skydance also laid out its entertainment leadership team on Monday morning. HBO boss Casey Bloys will run the content side of Skydance’s direct-to-consumer ventures, meaning HBO Max, Paramount+ and other streaming services. Paramount television boss George Cheeks will run the content side of the combined company’s sprawling TV operations. JB Perrette will run the business side of both those divisions. Paramount Pictures co-chairs Dana Goldberg and Josh Greenstein will oversee the combined company’s film businesses. James Gunn and Peter Safran will stay on as the co-heads of DC Studios. Ellison and Kreiz will hold an employee town hall on Tuesday followed by a media event later in the day.

title: Their jobs were among the first to be changed by AI. Now some are trying to avoid it
content: In 2024, software engineer Laura Housh began using AI as a helper for coding and other tasks. Two years later, Housh says she has a love-hate relationship with AI. “I’ve tried to use it for coding, and I just can’t get behind it,” she said. AI can provide direction or serve as a second set of eyes, she said, but added that it lacks the context to be truly useful. Housh isn’t the only one who thinks AI isn’t all that it’s cracked up to be. Six in 10 tech workers who participated in a new survey say they try to avoid using AI, according to Stack Overflow, a popular question-and-answer site for programmers. The results of Stack Overflow’s 103-question survey, which includes responses from 30,000 software developers in 169 countries, were shared exclusively with CNN ahead of their Tuesday publication. Software engineers have been at the forefront of the AI shift as one of the first industries to embrace the technology. Both tech giants and startups are increasingly using AI to write code, and “software developer” was ranked as the job most poised to be transformed by AI in an Indeed Hiring Lab report last year. The survey’s results, like Housh’s experience, provide a glimpse at what that transition has been like for some developers, painting a mixed picture of both rising adoption and uncertainty about how the technology is reshaping their professions. The Stack Overflow survey showed that 65% of responders use coding assistants or agents. Last year, Google’s research division published a survey of 5,000 tech professionals from around the world and found that 90% said they use AI in their job — a 14% increase from 2024. But job unhappiness among respondents in Stack Overflow’s survey has also grown compared to last year. Nearly one in three said they are not happy in their current roles, compared to 28.4% last year. About 45% described themselves as “complacent” with their jobs and only 22.3% are “happy.” The biggest factors among those who are complacent or unhappy are burnout, tech fatigue, economic uncertainty and a lack of clarity about upward mobility in their role. Many of those anxieties would exist regardless of AI. But the fast pace of AI advancement has “augmented” some of those concerns, according to Stack Overflow CEO Prashanth Chandrasekar. “People have to completely retool their jobs, and so it is quite unnerving for folks to know exactly how much of what they’re doing will be automated,” Chandrasekar told CNN. Software developers are grappling with concerns that are more nuanced than whether their jobs will be replaced, according to Chandrasekar. Senior programmers may feel the skills they’ve honed are no longer as relevant, he said. Entry-level workers are expected to operate as if they have three years of experience since “the bar has been raised” because of AI. Tech workers often use their spare time to learn the latest coding tools, he said. Housh says she’s familiar with the pressures of learning and keeping up with AI. She said she watches AI-focused videos and reads platform documentation in her personal time — and she still struggles to keep up. “It’s taxing because you have a lot of noise saying, ‘Do this, do this, do this, or you’ll get left behind,’” she said. For programmers like Housh and Audrey Eschright, a software engineer with 20 years of experience, it’s not about a lack of desire to embrace the new technology. Rather, the problem is that AI agents have neither the broad general knowledge of an experienced developer nor the job-specific context of a longtime employee. That can cause friction and more fatigue for developers, said Housh. What’s more, using AI instead of writing code manually can leave developers out of the loop of the solution, Eschright said . “Writing code is how you solve problems,” said Eschright. “As a software engineer, the process of figuring out what a system does is to change it.” This sentiment is also captured in Stack Overflow’s survey results. A little more than 74% of respondents said AI is useful for implementing code, and about 72% said it’s helpful for debugging — but only 34.4% say AI is useful for other job functions like communication and design. The survey showed that just 6.6% trust AI with important decisions. And about 78% said that source attribution is important when checking AI-generated code. Developers are particularly careful about trusting AI today because the stakes are higher as more companies move AI projects from the pilot phase to mainstream use, according to Chandrasekar. A January report from Deloitte found 54% of the 3,200-plus business and IT leaders it surveyed expected to move 40% or more of their AI experiments into production in the next three to six months. “I don’t like losing control; I like critical thinking and curiosity,” said Housh. “It’s just so important to be more curious than ever.”

title: Anthropic expected to IPO despite market uncertainty, AI slowdown calls
content: Wall Street is gearing up for Anthropic’s expected mega initial public offering, a major test of investors’ appetite for one of the AI industry’s leading firms. Just weeks ago, its CEO called for an industry-wide slowdown over growing safety concerns. The IPO could take place as soon as November. Anthropic’s IPO has been highly anticipated after the company announced in June that it confidentially filed to go public. Anthropic could raise as much as $100 billion in an IPO that would value the company at around $2 trillion, according to the Journal. The seismic sums would vault Anthropic into the top 10 most valuable companies in the world. Anthropic’s IPO would mark a major milestone in the AI boom that has enveloped markets in recent years. But the journey to the IPO has been messy, and there have been delays. Anthropic’s plans have been muddled by questions about AI regulation and safety risks. Former employees, as well as CEO Dario Amodei, have raised concerns in recent weeks, spurring an industry-wide call to slow down AI development to better manage risks. Tech leaders, including Amodei, signed an accord at the White House last week to “self-police” the development of AI. Meanwhile, the outlook for all potential IPOs has grown complicated in recent months. The market has grown more uncertain as interest rates are on the rise. Bond yields have surged in recent weeks, pushing up borrowing costs, as traders adjust to the Iran war energy shock and central banks raising rates. Some companies have gotten cold feet. Oura, a tech company that makes wearable health tracking rings, said it would go public this fall before announcing last week that it would delay its debut due to market uncertainty. Holtec Nuclear, an energy company, also recently suspended its planned IPO, citing poor sentiment impacting the stock market. And OpenAI announced it would delay its IPO until next year because of AI safety concerns. “You’ve got rising rates. You’ve got the war in Iran. You’ve got the sort of shakier economy ex-AI,” Heath Terry, head of AI investment research at Citi, told CNN. “I think that’s what’s sort of created uncertainty.” “IPOs need a stable market environment, they need positive investor sentiment, and with that sort of unstable broader economic landscape, that makes it a lot more difficult,” Terry said, speaking broadly about IPOs and not specific companies. Still, Anthropic is reportedly moving forward with its plans to go public while it raises capital. Should Anthropic raise $100 billion and debut at a valuation of around $2 trillion, it would surpass SpaceX’s IPO as the largest ever. SpaceX ultimately raised roughly $86 billion in its IPO and debuted at a $1.77 trillion valuation, partly due to visions for its own role in AI. The mega-sized SpaceX IPO trounced previous public offerings, with Saudi Aramco a distant No. 2, after it raised roughly $29 billion in 2019. “SpaceX was such an outlier — the world’s biggest IPO ever, by far. And it’s very possible that they’ll be in second place (roughly) a month from now,” said Jay Ritter, professor emeritus at the University of Florida. To be sure, the risk of AI taking over the world has been discussed for years. But scrutiny intensified in recent weeks after multiple incidents of AI agents going rogue and trying to hack into other systems. Reuters last week obtained a copy of Anthropic’s IPO prospectus, which has yet to be released, and reported that it includes warnings that the company’s AI model could potentially cause a “catastrophic or existential risk to humanity.” While tech leaders have agreed to self-police, Anthropic is still expected to grow its business and compete with rivals like OpenAI. Heightened safety concerns would exist whether the company went public or not, experts told CNN. Higher interest rates can also depress valuations for stocks and put a chill on the IPO market. But waiting to go public doesn’t guarantee interest rates will fall, and for a company that’s hungry for cash like Anthropic, going public can still make sense, said analysts and Ritter, the professor emeritus at the University of Florida. Delaying an IPO indefinitely also carries the risk that market conditions get worse, or other unforeseen challenges arise, and it becomes more difficult to get back on track toward an IPO. At the same time, the Nasdaq Composite is currently trading near a record high, which is a positive scenario for a tech IPO. “You can’t really ever time an IPO to eliminate all future uncertainty with respect to your company and your product,” Jill E. Fisch, professor of business law at the University of Pennsylvania Carey Law School, told CNN. “I don’t think there’s a magic line for any company in terms of, ‘Yes, now we’ve crossed the threshold, we’ve solved all of the safety issues, and now we can go forward with 100% confidence.’ I don’t think it really works that way,” Fisch said. Anthropic and OpenAI are in a heated race to produce advanced AI models, and the companies are burning billions in cash to advance research and development. Anthropic lost $42 billion in 2025 and plans to spend north of $500 billion on computing and infrastructure in the coming years, according to Reuters. However, the company reportedly told investors that it will be profitable for a second straight quarter this year, according to the Financial Times. Anthropic builds its revenue by renting out advanced models of its Claude bot to major businesses. Angelo Zino, tech analyst at CFRA Research, said that while the market conditions might not be conducive to every company’s plans to go public, he thinks Anthropic is in a league of its own. He cited strong signs of demand for its products and a path to profitability despite the company’s enormous capital spending. “I think there’s going to be a very strong appetite and demand for Anthropic,” Zino said. AI has been the central theme propelling the stock market to record highs in recent years. At its stratospheric valuation, Anthropic is asking investors to believe in its ability to continue monetizing its AI services and expand its market share. “If the company executes its business model, it’s going to do fine,” said Ritter, the professor emeritus at the University of Florida. “But you know, a lot of times things don’t work out.”
